title: The gold ring and the filthy coat
hook: who gets the good seat? James, Jesus' guest list, and a love of preference for the poor
carry: a preferential love for the poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first job in Genesis: look after the ground. Your line was till and keep.

Two visitors come through the door of the meeting at the same moment. One wears a gold ring and fine clothes. The other wears a filthy coat. Someone hurries over to the first and says, in the old King James words, "Sit thou here in a good place." To the second: "Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool." That scene is in the letter of James, and James asks his readers straight out whether they've started sorting people by their clothes. Underneath sits a plain question that any gathering answers, whether it means to or not: who gets the good seat?

Jesus answers the seat question at a dinner party in Luke's Gospel. Watching guests elbow toward the best places, he turns to the host with advice for next time: "call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind." And the reason: "for they cannot recompense thee." A guest list built on who can invite you back is a trade. A guest list that starts with the poor is a gift. Catholic teaching gives this a name, often called the preferential option for the poor; the Catholic catechism speaks of the poor as the object of the Church's preferential love. It doesn't mean God loves rich people less, or that being poor makes anyone holy. It means that when choices get made, about money, time, laws or who sits where, the needs of the poor are weighed first. Other churches arrive there by their own roads. John Wesley, the Anglican preacher behind the Methodist movement, preached a sermon on visiting the sick, pressing his hearers to go in person, not only to send help. Sending help is good, he said, but going yourself teaches what sending can't. You meet the people themselves: their faces, their names, what their week is actually like. So "first" turns out to be practical: the good seat, the top of the budget, and on an ordinary Tuesday, an hour given to someone who can't pay it back.

Bring to mind one person you know, or pass often, who is struggling to get by: a neighbor between jobs, a relative behind on rent, the man on the same corner every morning. Notice whether you know their name, and let them sit in the front row of your mind for a while, ahead of your own errands. If you pray, you can hold them before God, by name, or by face if you don't know the name.
The poor first. When choices are made about money, time or a seat at the table, the needs of the poor are weighed before anyone else's.
Your line: a preferential love for the poor. First means the seat, the budget and your time. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians live this out through church food pantries, shelters and visiting ministries; Catholic social teaching names it the preferential option for the poor, and Methodist and other churches teach personal visiting alongside giving.

fork.setup: you're greeting people at the door. a man with a gold ring and a man in a filthy coat walk in together, and there's one good seat left. what do you do?
options: give the good seat to the man with the ring.
give the good seat to the man in the filthy coat.
point them both to the back and let them sort it out.
fork.reveal: James condemns giving the good place to the rich and sending the poor to stand, and Jesus tells hosts to call the poor first. the text's answer is the man in the filthy coat.

original.note: Greek: poor, often in the sense of a beggar; the word used in James 2 and Luke 14.

chat.says: Does putting the poor first mean God loves rich people less?
options: No. It means that when choices get made, the needs of the poor are weighed first.
Yes. In Catholic teaching the rich are loved less, so the poor get the good seat.
No. It means being poor makes a person holy, so they deserve the best place.
chat.meaning: Catholic teaching calls it a preferential love: not loving anyone less, and not saying poverty makes anyone holy, but weighing the needs of the poor first.

tie.story: James pictures a church giving the good seat to a man with a gold ring and telling the man in a filthy coat to stand.
tie.friend: Your coworker can hear that putting the poor first isn't God loving the rich less; it's whose needs get weighed first.
tie.you: Who could get your good seat this week?

notes: The outline's hook says Wesley visited the poor weekly; that claim was left out under the claims rule. The script says only that his sermon 'On Visiting the Sick' presses hearers to visit in person and not only send help, and that going teaches what money can't. Confirm the paraphrase and the sermon number.

CCC 2448 speaks of the Church's 'love of preference for the poor'; the phrase 'preferential option for the poor' is the common name in Catholic social teaching. Confirm the paraphrase and that the explanation (not that God loves the rich less, nor that poverty makes anyone holy) fairly states Catholic teaching.
James 2:2 'assembly' renders Greek synagōgē; confirm the trapdoor floor.
John Wesley described as 'the Anglican preacher behind the Methodist movement'; confirm wording.
Luke 14:12–14 is set at a meal in a Pharisee's house; the script says only 'a dinner party' and does not cast the host as a foil.
